summary: A passage from a novel (Book 11, part 61) in which Rebecca, a young soap saleswoman, chats with a well-dressed gentleman at a farmhouse porch. She sells him on the purity of her soap, and their talk turns to childhood hardships, with Rebecca reporting her own poverty and the stranger hinting at a sad past. The excerpt ends as Rebecca begins explaining that she and her silent partner, who holds the horse at the gate, are not selling for their own profit.
one_line: Rebecca, a young soap seller, bonds with a wealthy-looking stranger on a farm porch, trading stories of unhappy childhoods.
key_facts: Rebecca is a young soap agent who promotes two soaps, the Rose-Red and the Snow-White.
The soap is described as made from pure vegetable fats with no acid in it, and a child could do the Monday washing with it using no force.
The gentleman is staying at his aunt's house while she is away in Portland.
The gentleman says he used to live on this farm as a boy and is very fond of the spot.
Rebecca says nothing takes the place of the farm where one lived as a child.
Rebecca says her childhood trouble was no shoes, too many babies and not enough books.
The gentleman says his worst childhood trouble was lack of food and clothes principally.
Rebecca notices the gentleman's eyes are tired and his mouth is sad when he is not speaking, despite his handsome, well-fed, prosperous look.
Rebecca has a silent partner who is holding the horse at the gate.
Rebecca explains that she and her partner are not selling for their own benefit.
Rebecca offers to check the printed circular to see how much soap the aunt needs.
